Dublin 2040: How Much Power, How Many Substations, What Budget?

Mankirat Singh · Portfolio · GitHub · LinkedIn

County Dublin (Dublin City, Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown). Data: CSO metered electricity consumption and Census 2022 (heating, cars, population by electoral division); ESB Networks Demand Capacity Headroom Report and customer heatmap. 2040 is the year of ESB's Net Zero strategy. Independent analysis, not an ESB or ESB Networks publication.

Key findings

  • County Dublin used 6,500 GWh of electricity in 2025, equivalent to a winter peak of about 1,124 MW.
  • By 2040 the peak could reach 2,414 MW in the central case (+115%), and 1,519–3,841 MW across scenarios. The biggest single driver is heat pumps, with about 317,740 extra heat pumps and 459,866 extra electric cars.
  • 77 of 113 Dublin 110 kV / 38 kV substations would run short of capacity by 2040 (central case).
  • Meeting it needs about 24 new substations (10–90% range 16–46) plus about 80 upgrades, costing €379–817m in station investment alone (2026 prices).
  • Flexibility pays: smart EV charging, heat-pump flexibility and demand response cut the 2040 peak to 2,083 MW and the median station bill by about €203m (12 new stations instead of 24).
  • ESB Networks' own station forecasts point the same way: in 2040 Aggressive 74, Base 70, Best View 67, Conservative 60 Dublin stations have no firm spare capacity left.

1. Where Dublin starts

Yearly consumption is turned into a winter peak with a load factor of 0.66 (average ÷ peak), the quantity that sizes substations.

2. How much power Dublin will need

The model adds, year by year: new homes and people, business growth, heat pumps (new homes plus conversions of oil-, gas- and solid-fuel-heated homes, mapped from Census 2022), electric cars (from Census car ownership), and new large loads, minus efficiency gains. Heat pumps and EVs follow an S-shaped uptake curve.

Data centres. The CSO reports that data centres used 23% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2025, much of it in the Dublin area. This model does not try to split existing data-centre use out of the CSO county figure above; the separate data-centre driver covers only new data-centre and large-user load from 2025 (central +250 MW by 2040). It counts towards Dublin's peak, but these sites connect mostly to the transmission grid (EirGrid), so it is not assigned to ESB Networks' 110 kV and 38 kV distribution stations below.

4. Which substations run out

Each electoral division's extra 2040 load is assigned to its nearest 110 kV or 38 kV station and compared with that station's spare capacity today (ESB Networks data). Only stations on ESB Networks' demand list take new load; generation-only stations such as wind farms and hydro are excluded. A small shortfall is met by upgrading the station (for example larger transformers); a larger one is met by upgrading it and adding new station(s) nearby for the rest.

How this compares: the central case here finds 77 stations short, closest to ESB Networks' Aggressive scenario (74). It is more demanding than all four, mainly because it assumes faster heat-pump and EV uptake to meet the 2040 net-zero path, and uses today's spare capacity from the heatmap rather than ESB Networks' planned reinforcements.

8. How Dublin can accommodate it

  • Flexibility first. Smart EV charging and heat-pump flexibility are the cheapest "capacity": they defer or avoid stations (section 5). Time-of-use tariffs and managed charging should be in place before EV numbers peak.
  • Build where it runs out first. Stations that fill earliest (section 4) set the order of work; planning and consenting a 110 kV station takes years, so decisions are needed well before the year a station is full.
  • Upgrade before building. Where the shortfall is small, a larger transformer at an existing site is faster and cheaper than a new station.
  • Plan with the councils. Growth is concentrated in Dublin City and its expansion areas; reserving sites and cable routes in development plans now avoids costly retrofits later.
  • Treat data centres as a transmission and flexibility question. New large users need EirGrid connections and, under the CRU's large energy user policy, on-site generation or demand flexibility; shared planning with ESB Networks keeps them from crowding out homes and heat pumps.
  • Keep the plan live. Re-run yearly as ESB Networks updates its workbooks and CSO publishes new data.

Limitations and methods

  • Consumption is metered energy by county; the winter peak is estimated with a load factor, not measured. Business and industry growth, new large loads, and EV charging behaviour are the least certain inputs.
  • Station assignment uses straight-line distance to the nearest station, a simplification of real network topology; ESB Networks' spare-capacity figures are indicative and can be limited by upstream circuits.
  • Costs cover stations only and use public examples and stated assumptions, not ESB Networks unit costs.
  • Methods: Python (pandas, NumPy, matplotlib). Bottom-up scenario model by electoral division with S-curve technology uptake; nearest-station spatial assignment; 5,000-run Monte Carlo over demand drivers, station sizes and unit costs (triangular distributions); one-at-a-time sensitivity; automatic reading of ESB Networks workbooks with structure detection and Irish Transverse Mercator conversion. Code: GitHub.
Data: CSO (CC BY 4.0); ESB Networks (DNDP). Analysis and any errors are the author's own.
